A01: Reference SQL ↔ pandas translation sheet Browse every method and its linked examples → Translate the operation, not just the syntax This is an authored cross-reference to the patterns used throughout SQLBolt and the supplied exercises. A similar-looking pandas expression is not automatically equivalent: row grain, missing values, duplicates and order must agree. SQL pandas pattern Watch for SELECT a, b df[['a', 'b']] A list preserves a DataFrame; projection does not deduplicate. WHERE a > 3 AND b = 1 df.loc[df['a'].gt(3) & df['b'].eq(1)] Use elementwise & / |, not Python and / or. IS NULL / IS NOT NULL s.isna() / s.notna() Never test SQL NULL using = NULL. IN ('A','B') s.isin(['A','B']) NOT IN and missing values require explicit care. SELECT DISTINCT a df[['a']].drop_duplicates() Deduplicate only the columns that form the result. ORDER BY a DESC, b df.sort_values(['a','b'], ascending=[False,True]) Add a unique tie-break when a single deterministic row is required. LIMIT 5 OFFSET 10 sorted_df.iloc[10:15] Sort before selecting a page. INNER / LEFT JOIN left.merge(right, on='id', how='inner'/'left') Validate expected one-to-one or many-to-one cardinality. COUNT(*) / COUNT(x) groupby.size() / groupby[x].count() size counts rows; count ignores missing x. COUNT(DISTINCT x) groupby['x'].nunique() Distinct nonmissing values. SUM(x) groupby['x'].sum(min_count=1) Use min_count=1 when an all-missing group must stay missing. GROUP BY k df.groupby('k', dropna=False) SQL retains a NULL grouping key; default pandas groupby drops it. HAVING SUM(x) > 0 Aggregate, then filter the aggregated frame. Do not confuse this with a pre-aggregation WHERE. MIN(x) OVER (PARTITION BY k) df.groupby('k')['x'].transform('min') transform broadcasts the statistic to every source row. DENSE_RANK() OVER (...) groupby['x'].rank(method='dense', ascending=False) Use the ranking method that preserves the intended ties. LAG / LEAD with ORDER BY Sort, then groupby.shift(1) / shift(-1). A previous row is not necessarily the previous calendar day. SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY t ROWS ...) Sort, then cumsum(). A cumulative total differs from a grouped total. UNION ALL / UNION concat(...) / concat(...).drop_duplicates() Align selected columns; SQL uses positions and pandas uses names. CASE WHEN condition ... Boolean masks with where/map. Keep NULL behavior and labels explicit. UPDATE / DELETE Assign with .loc / retain the complement mask. A DataFrame change does not update the database. A tiny aggregation example pandas Copy visits = pd . DataFrame ({ 'shop' : [ 'A' , 'A' , 'B' ], 'amount' : [ 10 , 20 , None ]}) result = visits . groupby ( 'shop' , dropna = False )[ 'amount' ] . sum ( min_count = 1 ) . reset_index () Result: shop A has 30; shop B remains missing. Without min_count=1, the all-missing B group would become zero, unlike SQL SUM. Three important non-equivalences Missing merge keys: pandas can match missing keys to each other; SQL equality joins do not. Group keys: SQL groups NULL keys together, while pandas needs dropna=False to retain them. Logical complements: NOT(condition) in SQL can still be unknown for a NULL row, whereas a pandas negation may include it depending on dtype and expression. pandas SQL comparison — Projection, filtering, grouping, joins and operations. pandas merge — Join modes, cardinality validation and missing-key behavior. pandas groupby — Aggregation, transform and missing groups. MySQL windows — Ordering and window expressions. ← Previous About these notes Next → Setup and conventions
A02: Reference Setup and conventions One problem at a time Every exercise has its own tables. SQLBolt examples use its tutorial schema; the Leetcode SQL targets MySQL 8 or later. Do not combine unrelated examples into one database script. pandas The function examples accept DataFrames with the same column names as the exercise tables. Each practice implementation includes its imports. SQLBolt snippets assume import pandas as pd and lowercase DataFrame names matching their tables. Create the input DataFrames from the exercise data before calling a function. Date operations require datetime-like columns; use pd.to_datetime when loading dates as strings. Dates and order A previous row is not necessarily the previous calendar day. Sort before shifting or rolling, and use calendar-date comparisons when the task asks for days. A half-open month interval includes the start date and excludes the first day of the following month. Rounding Python and pandas normally round exact halfway values to the nearest even result. MySQL exact-value rounding uses halves away from zero. Where needed, the examples include this half-up helper. pandas Copy """Authored pandas study alternatives; see the corresponding pages for assumptions. Requires pandas. All functions return a new result except delete_duplicate_emails, which intentionally mutates its input. Synthetic tests are in ../tests/. """ from decimal import Decimal , ROUND_HALF_UP import pandas as pd def round_half_up ( value , digits : int = 2 ): """Round the decimal representation of value; preserve missing values. This does not recover precision already lost in binary floating-point arithmetic. For exact financial arithmetic, retain Decimal or integer minor units upstream. """ if pd . isna ( value ): return float ( 'nan' ) return float ( Decimal ( str ( value )) . quantize ( Decimal ( 1 ) . scaleb ( - digits ), rounding = ROUND_HALF_UP )) The helper rounds the decimal representation of its input. It does not undo floating-point precision loss; retain Decimal values or integer minor units when exact decimal arithmetic is required. B03: SQLBolt / Lesson 3 Text constraints and LIKE LIKE patterns use % for zero or more characters and _ for exactly one character. Equality matches a complete value. NOT LIKE excludes matching non-NULL values. Note. SQLBolt describes LIKE as case-insensitive in its environment. This is not a universal SQL rule: engine and collation matter. Pandas patterns below deliberately use case=False for LIKE; equality uses the supplied capitalization. 01 · Toy Story titles SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE 'Toy Story%' ; pandas result = movies . loc [ movies [ 'title' ] . str . contains ( r '^Toy Story' , case = False , na = False )] . copy () 02 · Movies by John Lasseter SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT * FROM movies WHERE director = 'John Lasseter' ; pandas result = movies . loc [ movies [ 'director' ] . eq ( 'John Lasseter' )] . copy () 03 · Movies by other directors SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT title , director FROM movies WHERE director <> 'John Lasseter' ; pandas mask = movies [ 'director' ] . notna () & movies [ 'director' ] . ne ( 'John Lasseter' ) result = movies . loc [ mask , [ 'title' , 'director' ]] . copy () 04 · WALL- followed by one character SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT * FROM movies WHERE title LIKE 'WALL-_' ; pandas result = movies . loc [ movies [ 'title' ] . str . fullmatch ( r 'WALL-.' , case = False , na = False )] . copy () The lesson’s WALL-* wording is implemented using the SQL single-character wildcard _. For an unrestricted suffix, use WALL-%. Sources The worked examples and pandas translations are study alternatives, not an official answer key. Shared DataFrame setup is listed under Reference. B06: SQLBolt / Lesson 6 INNER JOIN An INNER JOIN returns matching rows from both tables. Join movies.id to boxoffice.movie_id; qualify columns with aliases to make their origins clear. Note. The tutorial specifies one BoxOffice record per movie. The pandas validate argument checks that assumption; a many-to-many join would multiply rows. 01 · Domestic and international sales per movie SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT m . title , b . domestic_sales , b . international_sales FROM movies m JOIN boxoffice b ON m . id = b . movie_id ; pandas m = movies . merge ( boxoffice , left_on = 'id' , right_on = 'movie_id' , how = 'inner' , validate = 'one_to_one' ) result = m [[ 'title' , 'domestic_sales' , 'international_sales' ]] 02 · Movies with higher international sales SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT m . title , b . domestic_sales , b . international_sales FROM movies m JOIN boxoffice b ON m . id = b . movie_id WHERE b . international_sales > b . domestic_sales ; pandas m = movies . merge ( boxoffice , left_on = 'id' , right_on = 'movie_id' , how = 'inner' , validate = 'one_to_one' ) result = m . loc [ m [ 'international_sales' ] . gt ( m [ 'domestic_sales' ]), [ 'title' , 'domestic_sales' , 'international_sales' ]] 03 · Movies ordered by rating, highest first SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT m . title , b . rating FROM movies m JOIN boxoffice b ON m . id = b . movie_id ORDER BY b . rating DESC ; pandas m = movies . merge ( boxoffice , left_on = 'id' , right_on = 'movie_id' , how = 'inner' , validate = 'one_to_one' ) result = m . sort_values ( 'rating' , ascending = False )[[ 'title' , 'rating' ]] Sources The worked examples and pandas translations are study alternatives, not an official answer key. B08: SQLBolt / Lesson 8 NULL and unmatched rows IS NULL and IS NOT NULL test missing values. An unmatched outer-join row contains NULLs on the missing side. B09: SQLBolt / Lesson 9 Expressions and aliases Expressions calculate values in a query; AS gives the result a readable name. Arithmetic can convert units, combine sales or identify even years. Note. These tasks use the tutorial’s complete movie/boxoffice matches. A LEFT JOIN would be needed to retain movies with no BoxOffice row; do not silently treat unknown sales as zero. 01 · Combined sales in millions SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT m . title , ( b . domestic_sales + b . international_sales ) / 1000000 . 0 AS sales_millions FROM movies m JOIN boxoffice b ON m . id = b . movie_id ; pandas m = movies . merge ( boxoffice , left_on = 'id' , right_on = 'movie_id' , how = 'inner' , validate = 'one_to_one' ) result = m . assign ( sales_millions = ( m [ 'domestic_sales' ] + m [ 'international_sales' ]) / 1_000_000 )[[ 'title' , 'sales_millions' ]] 02 · Ratings as percentages SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT m . title , b . rating * 10 . 0 AS rating_percent FROM movies m JOIN boxoffice b ON m . id = b . movie_id ; pandas m = movies . merge ( boxoffice , left_on = 'id' , right_on = 'movie_id' , how = 'inner' , validate = 'one_to_one' ) result = m . assign ( rating_percent = m [ 'rating' ] * 10 )[[ 'title' , 'rating_percent' ]] 03 · Movies released in even years SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT title , year FROM movies WHERE year % 2 = 0 ; pandas result = movies . loc [ movies [ 'year' ] . mod ( 2 ) . eq ( 0 ), [ 'title' , 'year' ]] Sources The worked examples and pandas translations are study alternatives, not an official answer key. B10: SQLBolt / Lesson 10 Aggregates and GROUP BY Aggregates collapse rows into summary values. Without GROUP BY the entire input is one group; with GROUP BY there is one result per group. COUNT(*) counts rows, whereas COUNT(column) excludes NULL. Note. Pandas groupby drops missing group keys unless dropna=False. SUM in SQL returns NULL when no non-NULL values contribute; sum(min_count=1) preserves that distinction. 01 · Longest employee tenure SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT MAX ( years_employed ) AS max_years FROM employees ; pandas result = pd . DataFrame ({ 'max_years' : [ employees [ 'years_employed' ] . max ()]}) 02 · Mean tenure per role SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT role , AVG ( years_employed ) AS average_years FROM employees GROUP BY role ; pandas result = employees . groupby ( 'role' , dropna = False , as_index = False ) . agg ( average_years = ( 'years_employed' , 'mean' )) 03 · Total employee-years per building SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT building , SUM ( years_employed ) AS total_years FROM employees GROUP BY building ; pandas result = employees . groupby ( 'building' , dropna = False )[ 'years_employed' ] . sum ( min_count = 1 ) . reset_index ( name = 'total_years' ) Sum years_employed; counting employees answers a different question. A building with nobody assigned is absent unless buildings is left-joined first. Sources The worked examples and pandas translations are study alternatives, not an official answer key. B11: SQLBolt / Lesson 11 WHERE versus HAVING WHERE filters individual rows before aggregation. HAVING filters grouped results after aggregation. Choose the clause according to whether the condition describes an input row or a group result. Note. The engineer task can use WHERE before SUM. The HAVING form shown keeps the grouping concept visible; it does not imply that WHERE would be incorrect. 01 · Count artists without HAVING SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT COUNT ( * ) AS artist_count FROM employees WHERE role = 'Artist' ; pandas result = pd . DataFrame ({ 'artist_count' : [ int ( employees [ 'role' ] . eq ( 'Artist' ) . sum ())]}) 02 · Employee count per role SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT role , COUNT ( * ) AS employee_count FROM employees GROUP BY role ; pandas result = employees . groupby ( 'role' , dropna = False ) . size () . reset_index ( name = 'employee_count' ) 03 · Total engineer tenure SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT role , SUM ( years_employed ) AS total_years FROM employees GROUP BY role HAVING role = 'Engineer' ; pandas g = employees . groupby ( 'role' , dropna = False )[ 'years_employed' ] . sum ( min_count = 1 ) . reset_index ( name = 'total_years' ) result = g . loc [ g [ 'role' ] . eq ( 'Engineer' )] Sources The worked examples and pandas translations are study alternatives, not an official answer key. B12: SQLBolt / Lesson 12 Logical query order The lesson’s logical order is FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT/OFFSET. This explains which values and aliases are available to each clause. Note. This is a logical model, not a promise of the physical execution plan. Optimizers may transform execution. Window functions add another logical stage, covered in the reference pages. 01 · Film count per director SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT director , COUNT ( * ) AS movie_count FROM movies GROUP BY director ; pandas result = movies . groupby ( 'director' , dropna = False ) . size () . reset_index ( name = 'movie_count' ) 02 · Combined domestic and international revenue per director SQL pandas Copy SQL SELECT m . director , SUM ( b . domestic_sales + b . international_sales ) AS total_sales FROM movies m JOIN boxoffice b ON m . id = b . movie_id GROUP BY m . director ; pandas m = movies . merge ( boxoffice , left_on = 'id' , right_on = 'movie_id' , how = 'inner' , validate = 'one_to_one' ) m = m . assign ( total_sales = m [ 'domestic_sales' ] + m [ 'international_sales' ]) result = m . groupby ( 'director' , dropna = False )[ 'total_sales' ] . sum ( min_count = 1 ) . reset_index () Sources The worked examples and pandas translations are study alternatives, not an official answer key. /*
    SCHEMA for `player`:
    id	first_name	last_name	age	status	debt	    isinsider
    1	Luigi	    Mangione	27	alive	3930975804	false
    2	Seokjin	    Nam	        68	alive	684587725	false

*/

WITH
    table_prop AS (
        SELECT FLOOR( COUNT(*) * 0.9 ) AS portions
        FROM player
        WHERE status = 'alive' AND isinsider = false
    )

SELECT 
    table_prop.portions AS portions,
    CASE 
        WHEN table_prop.portions > rations.amount THEN 'False'
        ELSE 'True'
    END AS amount
FROM table_prop, rations Download level_02.sql ↓ Explore methods in these solutions SQL WHERE AND COUNT() CASE FLOOR() Subquery WITH SELECT pandas Select column Select columns Multiple conditions New column map() Fill null sum() eq() / ne() gt() / ge() / lt() / le() copy() ← Previous Filter the player pool Next → Compare hot and cold months

/*

WITH 
    Hesitation_game AS (
        SELECT game_id
        FROM Player
        WHERE death_description = 'pushed'
        GROUP BY game_id
        ORDER BY AVG(last_moved_time_seconds) DESC
        LIMIT 1
    )

SELECT 
    p.id, 
    p.first_name, 
    p.last_name,
    p.last_moved_time_seconds AS hesitation_time
FROM Player p
INNER JOIN Hesitation_game h
    ON p.game_id = h.game_id
WHERE p.death_description = 'pushed'
ORDER BY p.last_moved_time_seconds DESC

WITH 
	Most_recent_squid_game AS (
        SELECT start_time, end_time
        FROM Game_schedule
        WHERE LOWER(type) = 'squid game'
        ORDER BY date DESC
        LIMIT 1
	),
    Guards_on_shift AS (
        SELECT g.id, g.assigned_post, g.shift_start, g.shift_end
        FROM Guard g, Most_recent_squid_game m
        WHERE 
            (m.start_time BETWEEN g.shift_start and g.shift_end) OR 
            (m.end_time   BETWEEN g.shift_start and g.shift_end) OR 
            ((g.shift_start BETWEEN m.start_time and m.end_time) AND (g.shift_end BETWEEN m.start_time and m.end_time))
    ),
	Suspect AS (
		SELECT 
			g.id,
			g.assigned_post, 
			g.shift_start,
			g.shift_end, 
			d.access_time, 
			d.door_location
		FROM Guards_on_shift g
		INNER JOIN Daily_door_access_logs d
			ON g.id = d.guard_id
		WHERE g.assigned_post <> d.door_location
	)
	
SELECT g.id, d.access_time
FROM Guards_on_shift g
INNER JOIN Daily_door_access_logs d
    ON g.id = d.guard_id
WHERE 
    (d.access_time BETWEEN 
	   (select start_time from Most_recent_squid_game) and
	   (select end_time from Most_recent_squid_game)) AND
    (d.door_location IN (select door_location from Suspect)) Download level_09.sql ↓ Explore methods in these solutions SQL WHERE AND OR IN BETWEEN INNER JOIN LOWER() Subquery WITH SELECT ORDER BY LIMIT / OFFSET pandas Select column Rows by label Rows by position Multiple conditions OR Membership Range Non-missing Sort one column Descending New column Rename Access label Inner merge Lowercase Convert date astype() eq() / ne() gt() / ge() / lt() / le() copy() ← Previous Find the longest hesitation Contents All sections
